scope.level_definition: Mastery of all six included competencies represents the hard level for this bank.

sub_competencies.title: Python Programming
learning_items: Use Python collections, functions, comprehensions, iterators, and type hints to process data.
Organize AI code into reusable modules, classes, and packages.
Apply exception handling, logging, file handling, and configuration management.

sub_competencies.title: Clean and Testable Code
learning_items: Refactor an unstructured AI script into small, maintainable functions.
Write unit tests for preprocessing, inference, and utility functions.
Debug incorrect outputs using logs, stack traces, breakpoints, and controlled inputs.

sub_competencies.title: Development Workflow
learning_items: Use Git branches, commits, pull requests, and merge-conflict resolution.
Manage dependencies using virtual environments and dependency files.
Work with Linux commands, environment variables, and basic shell scripts.

sub_competencies.title: Data Collection and Storage
learning_items: Load data from CSV, JSON, databases, REST APIs, and document sources.
Query relational data using filtering, joins, aggregation, and grouping in SQL.
Select an appropriate storage format for structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data.

sub_competencies.title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
learning_items: Detect and handle missing values, duplicate records, outliers, and inconsistent formats.
Encode categorical variables and scale or normalize numerical variables.
Preprocess text, image, or document data for downstream AI models.

sub_competencies.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
learning_items: Calculate descriptive statistics and inspect data distributions.
Visualize relationships, trends, class imbalance, and unusual observations.
Identify data-quality risks, leakage, bias, and potentially unreliable features.

sub_competencies.title: Feature Engineering and Data Pipelines
learning_items: Create useful numerical, categorical, temporal, and text-based features.
Build a reproducible preprocessing pipeline.
Prevent training-serving skew by applying consistent transformations during training and inference.

sub_competencies.title: Problem Formulation
learning_items: Translate a business problem into classification, regression, clustering, ranking, or retrieval.
Define the target variable, input features, prediction unit, and success metric.
Recognize when rules, analytics, search, or a simple statistical model may be better than ML.

sub_competencies.title: Supervised Learning
learning_items: Train and explain basic regression and classification models.
Compare linear models, decision trees, ensembles, and nearest-neighbour methods.
Detect underfitting, overfitting, high bias, and high variance.

sub_competencies.title: Unsupervised Learning
learning_items: Apply clustering and interpret resulting groups.
Use dimensionality reduction for exploration or feature compression.
Evaluate whether unsupervised outputs are meaningful and stable.

sub_competencies.title: Model Evaluation and Selection
learning_items: Select suitable metrics such as precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, MAE, or RMSE.
Apply train-validation-test splitting and cross-validation correctly.
Compare models using performance, interpretability, latency, and operational cost.

sub_competencies.title: Experiment Design
learning_items: Establish a simple baseline before testing complex architectures.
Control random seeds, datasets, hyperparameters, and experiment configurations.
Record assumptions, model versions, metrics, and experiment results.

sub_competencies.title: Neural Network Implementation
learning_items: Explain layers, activations, loss functions, forward propagation, and backpropagation.
Implement a basic neural network using PyTorch or TensorFlow.
Build data loaders, training loops, validation loops, and model checkpoints.

sub_competencies.title: Model Improvement and Optimization
learning_items: Tune learning rate, batch size, model size, regularization, and training duration.
Diagnose failures using confusion matrices, prediction samples, and error categories.
Apply transfer learning or a pretrained model to a practical problem.

competencies.title: LLM, NLP, RAG and Agentic AI

sub_competencies.title: NLP and Embeddings
learning_items: Apply tokenization, text normalization, text classification, and information extraction.
Explain semantic embeddings and calculate similarity between vectors.
Select an embedding model based on language, domain, quality, latency, and cost.

sub_competencies.title: LLM APIs and Prompt Design
learning_items: Integrate an LLM API with appropriate authentication, parameters, and error handling.
Design prompts with clear instructions, context, constraints, and output schemas.
Generate and validate structured outputs such as JSON or typed objects.

sub_competencies.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
learning_items: Parse and chunk documents while preserving useful metadata.
Create embeddings, index documents, and retrieve relevant passages from a vector database.
Apply reranking, grounding, citation, and context assembly before generation.

sub_competencies.title: Agentic Workflows
learning_items: Define tools with clear inputs, outputs, permissions, and failure behaviour.
Implement tool calling, routing, retries, state management, and structured responses.
Add human approval for sensitive, uncertain, or irreversible agent actions.

sub_competencies.title: Model Adaptation and Inference
learning_items: Explain the difference between prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, and training from scratch.
Apply a basic fine-tuning method such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning when appropriate.
Compare hosted and open-weight models using quality, privacy, latency, hardware, and cost.

sub_competencies.title: Model and AI Service Deployment
learning_items: Expose an ML or LLM pipeline through a Flask or FastAPI endpoint.
Validate request and response schemas and return appropriate errors.
Package and run the service inside a Docker container.

sub_competencies.title: Reproducibility and Automation
learning_items: Version code, datasets, configurations, prompts, and models.
Separate training, evaluation, and inference into reproducible pipelines.
Run automated tests before merging or deploying changes.

sub_competencies.title: Monitoring and Operations
learning_items: Monitor availability, errors, latency, throughput, token usage, and cost.
Track model quality, retrieval quality, drift, and abnormal inputs.
Diagnose a production failure using logs, traces, metrics, and recent changes.

mcq.stem: A stack data structure provides which element-access order?
options: LIFO, last-in-first-out
FIFO, first-in-first-out
Random access by numeric index
Sorted / priority order by key
mcq.rationale: A stack is last-in-first-out: the most recently pushed element is the first one popped. FIFO describes a queue, index access describes an array, and priority ordering describes a heap.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confusing a stack with a queue (FIFO)
Confusing a stack with an indexable array
Confusing a stack with a priority queue / heap

mcq.stem: In Python, what is the difference between the `is` operator and the `==` operator?
options: `==` tests object identity while `is` tests value equality
`is` tests whether two references point to the same object; `==` tests value equality
`is` and `==` are interchangeable and always return the same result
`is` compares types while `==` compares memory addresses
mcq.rationale: `is` checks identity (whether two names refer to the same object in memory), while `==` checks equality of value (via `__eq__`). They can disagree, e.g. two distinct lists with equal contents.
misconceptions: Swapping the definitions of `is` and `==`
CORRECT
Believing the two operators are always equivalent
Misdescribing `is` as a type check and `==` as an address comparison

mcq.stem: Which precondition must hold for binary search to work correctly?
options: The collection must be implemented as a linked list
All elements in the collection must be unique
The collection must be sorted by the search key
The entire collection must fit in the CPU cache
mcq.rationale: Binary search relies on the data being sorted so it can discard half the range each step. It also needs random access (so a linked list is a poor fit), does not require uniqueness, and has no cache requirement.
misconceptions: Believing binary search needs a linked list, when it actually needs random access
Assuming elements must be unique, which is not required
CORRECT
Inventing an irrelevant hardware constraint

mcq.stem: A generator `g = (x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3])` is converted to a list twice. What are the two results?
options: `[2, 4, 6]` both times
A `TypeError` is raised on the second conversion
mcq.rationale: Generator iterators are consumed as values are requested; after the first `list(g)`, the generator is exhausted rather than automatically restarted.
misconceptions: Reflects a plausible misconception: `[2, 4, 6]` both times
Reflects a plausible misconception: `[]` and then `[2, 4, 6]`
Reflects a plausible misconception: A `TypeError` is raised on the second conversion
CORRECT

mcq.stem: Which expression returns `0` when key `"count"` is absent without modifying dictionary `d`?
options: `d["count"] or 0`
`d.get("count", 0)`
`d.setdefault("count", 0)`
`getattr(d, "count", 0)`
mcq.rationale: `dict.get` returns the provided default without inserting it. Indexing may raise `KeyError`; `setdefault` mutates the dictionary; `getattr` reads attributes, not keys.
misconceptions: Reflects a plausible misconception: `d["count"] or 0`
CORRECT
Reflects a plausible misconception: `d.setdefault("count", 0)`
Reflects a plausible misconception: `getattr(d, "count", 0)`

mcq.stem: Which statement about standard Python type hints is most accurate?
options: They prevent a function from receiving values of another type
They are ignored by IDEs but enforced by the interpreter
They primarily support static analysis and documentation; Python does not enforce them automatically at runtime
They convert incoming values to the annotated type before the function runs
mcq.rationale: Annotations are metadata unless a library or custom runtime validation explicitly interprets them.
misconceptions: Reflects a plausible misconception: They prevent a function from receiving values of another type
Reflects a plausible misconception: They are ignored by IDEs but enforced by the interpreter
CORRECT
Reflects a plausible misconception: They convert incoming values to the annotated type before the function runs

mcq.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
mcq.rationale: Merge sort always divides the input into halves (log n levels) and does O(n) merging work at each level, giving O(n log n) in the worst case, unlike quicksort whose worst case degrades to O(n^2).
misconceptions: Confusing merge sort with quicksort's O(n^2) worst case
Assuming sorting can be done in linear time by comparison
Confusing total work with the O(log n) recursion depth
CORRECT

mcq.stem: When two distinct keys hash to the same bucket in a hash table (a collision), which is a standard resolution strategy?
options: Chaining (each bucket holds a list of entries) or open addressing (probing for another slot)
Rehash the entire table on every insertion
Silently discard the more recently inserted key
Convert the whole table into a sorted array
mcq.rationale: Collisions are handled either by chaining (storing colliding entries in a per-bucket list) or by open addressing (probing to find another open slot). Full rehashing every insert would be needlessly expensive, and no correct implementation drops keys.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confusing occasional resize/rehash with a per-insertion rehash
Believing collisions cause silent data loss
Confusing a hash table with a sorted structure

mcq.stem: What does `funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]`; then `[f() for f in funcs]` return?

Reflects a plausible misconception: `[0, 0, 0]`

mcq.stem: A class defines a read-only `@property` named `score` with no setter. What usually happens on `obj.score = 10`?

The property getter is replaced on that instance
The assignment silently updates the getter's return value
`AttributeError` is raised because the data descriptor rejects assignment
mcq.rationale: A property object implements descriptor assignment behavior; without a setter, assigning to that attribute raises an error rather than creating a shadowing field.

Reflects a plausible misconception: The property getter is replaced on that instance
Reflects a plausible misconception: The assignment silently updates the getter's return value

mcq.stem: An `async def` FastAPI handler calls a CPU-heavy pure-Python function directly for 30 seconds. What is the most likely effect?
options: It blocks the event-loop thread, delaying other requests handled by that worker
It automatically runs on all CPU cores
The `await` keyword is inserted implicitly
It affects only the calling request because async functions always run in separate threads
mcq.rationale: Declaring a function async does not make CPU work non-blocking; the computation must be offloaded or moved to another process/service.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Reflects a plausible misconception: It automatically runs on all CPU cores
Reflects a plausible misconception: The `await` keyword is inserted implicitly
Reflects a plausible misconception: It affects only the calling request because async functions always run in separate threads

mcq.stem: In OOP, if class `Dog` inherits from class `Animal`, which statement is true?
options: `Animal` gains the methods defined in `Dog`
`Dog` inherits the attributes and methods defined in `Animal`
Every instance of `Animal` is also an instance of `Dog`
`Dog` may not define any new methods of its own
mcq.rationale: A subclass inherits the members of its base class, so `Dog` gets `Animal`'s attributes and methods and may also add or override its own. Inheritance flows base-to-derived, and the is-a relationship runs Dog is-an Animal, not the reverse.
misconceptions: Reversing the direction of inheritance
CORRECT
Reversing the is-a relationship between base and subclass
Believing a subclass cannot extend the base with new members

mcq.stem: What does the `@property` decorator let you do in a Python class?
options: Make an attribute globally accessible from other modules
Define a method that is accessed like an attribute, enabling computed or validated attribute access
Automatically persist the attribute's value to disk
Mark an attribute as a constant that can never be reassigned
mcq.rationale: `@property` turns a method into a managed attribute: reading `obj.x` runs the getter, and optional setter/deleter methods allow validation or computed values while keeping attribute-style syntax. It does not affect module scope, persistence, or immutability.
misconceptions: Confusing a property with module-level global visibility
CORRECT
Imagining an automatic persistence mechanism
Assuming a property makes an attribute a read-only constant (a setter can allow writes)

mcq.angle: undoing a pushed commit on a shared branch safely
mcq.stem: A bad commit has already been pushed to a shared branch that teammates have pulled. What is the safe way to undo its effect?
options: `git reset --hard` to the previous commit, then force-push
`git revert` the commit, creating a new commit that undoes its changes
`git checkout` the previous commit and keep committing from detached HEAD
Delete the `.git` folder and re-clone the repository
mcq.rationale: `git revert` records a new commit that reverses the bad one without rewriting shared history, so collaborators can simply pull. Resetting and force-pushing rewrites history others already have, causing divergence; a detached-HEAD checkout does not advance the branch; deleting `.git` loses local work and fixes nothing.
misconceptions: Rewriting shared history with reset + force-push, which breaks collaborators' clones
CORRECT
Confusing detached-HEAD checkout with updating the branch pointer
Resorting to a destructive re-clone that does not undo the commit

mcq.angle: cooperative super() and the C3 method resolution order
mcq.stem: In `class D(B, C)` where both `B` and `C` inherit from `A`, if every class calls `super().__init__()` cooperatively, what does Python's C3-linearized MRO guarantee about the `__init__` calls?
options: `A.__init__` runs twice, once reached through `B` and once through `C`
Only `B.__init__` runs and `C.__init__` is skipped entirely
Each class's `__init__` in the MRO runs exactly once, in the linearized order
The MRO is depth-first left-to-right, so `A.__init__` runs before `C.__init__`
mcq.rationale: With cooperative `super()` calls, C3 linearization gives the order D, B, C, A, and each `__init__` runs exactly once. This is precisely what avoids the classic diamond problem where a naively chained hierarchy would invoke the shared base twice.
misconceptions: Describing the naive non-cooperative diamond bug where the shared base is initialized twice
Assuming the second parent in the bases list is skipped
CORRECT
Applying the old pre-2.3 depth-first MRO, which C3 replaced for new-style classes

voice.angle: Mutable vs immutable objects and the mutable-default-argument trap
voice.question: Explain the difference between mutable and immutable objects in Python, and walk me through why using a mutable object like a list as a default function argument is a classic bug. What would you do instead?
voice.sample_strong_answer: Immutable objects like ints, strings, and tuples can't be changed in place; when you 'modify' them you actually rebind the name to a new object. Mutable objects like lists, dicts, and sets can be changed in place, so two names can point at the same object and see each other's mutations. The classic bug is writing def f(x, acc=[]): the default list is created once, when the function is defined, not on each call. So every call that relies on the default shares the same list, and it accumulates state across calls, which surprises people. The fix is the sentinel pattern: default the argument to None, and inside the function do if acc is None: acc = [] so you get a fresh list each call. The same idea applies to dicts and any mutable default. It matters because it's a subtle source of state leakage that unit tests sometimes miss when they only call the function once.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly defines mutable vs immutable with concrete type examples
Explains that default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time
Identifies the shared-state / accumulation symptom across calls
Gives the None-sentinel fix pattern
Notes this generalises to dicts and other mutable defaults
Connects it to real debugging or testing implications

rubric_criteria.descriptor: Mutability definitions, the once-at-definition evaluation model, and the sentinel fix are all technically correct
Covers definition, the bug mechanism, the symptom, and the fix rather than only naming the trap
Explains WHY the default is shared (definition-time evaluation) rather than just asserting the rule
Clear, well-sequenced spoken explanation a junior could follow

common_pitfalls: Claiming the default is re-evaluated on every call
Confusing mutability with variable scope or the global keyword
Proposing to 'just clear the list at the start' which still mutates a shared object
Giving the definition but never explaining the actual bug mechanism
Saying tuples are immutable but forgetting they can hold mutable elements when pressed

voice.angle: Big-O notation and why asymptotic complexity matters
voice.question: Explain what Big-O notation measures and why it matters when you write code. Contrast a couple of common complexities like O(1), O(n), and O(n squared) with a concrete example.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Big-O describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input size grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms, so it captures scaling behaviour rather than exact timings on one machine. O(1) is constant, the work doesn't grow with input, like a dictionary lookup by key. O(n) is linear, like scanning a list once to find a maximum, double the input and you roughly double the work. O(n squared) is quadratic, typical of nested loops comparing every pair, like a naive check for duplicates where you compare each element to every other, so ten times the data is a hundred times the work. It matters because an approach that feels fine on a hundred rows can be unusable on a million, and the difference between quadratic and linear or n-log-n often decides whether a feature is viable. In practice I use it to choose the right data structure, for example replacing a repeated linear membership test in a list with a set for O(1) lookups, which turns an accidental quadratic into linear. I'd also note Big-O hides constants, so for small inputs a 'worse' algorithm can be faster, and worst case versus average case can differ.
evaluation_criteria: Defines Big-O as growth of time/space with input size, dropping constants
Correctly characterises O(1), O(n), O(n^2) with examples
Explains why scaling matters for real workloads
Connects complexity to data-structure choice
Acknowledges constants/small-input caveats or worst-vs-average case

voice.question: Explain how a Python decorator works in terms of closures and first-class functions. Walk me through what happens when a function is decorated, and why we typically use functools.wraps.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Decorators lean on two facts: functions are first-class objects you can pass around and return, and closures let an inner function capture variables from the enclosing scope. A decorator is just a callable that takes a function and returns a replacement function. When you write @timer above def work(), Python evaluates that as work = timer(work) at definition time. Inside timer I define a wrapper closure that closes over the original function, does something before and after, for example records start and end time, calls the original, and returns its result. The name work now points at wrapper. The subtlety is that wrapper's metadata, its __name__, __doc__, and signature, replaces the original's, which breaks introspection, logging, and some frameworks. functools.wraps is itself a decorator you apply to wrapper that copies that metadata across so the decorated function still looks like the original. For decorators that take arguments you add one more layer: a factory that takes the args and returns the actual decorator. I'd use them for cross-cutting concerns like timing, caching, auth checks, or retries, keeping that logic out of the business function.

Gives realistic cross-cutting use cases

voice.angle: Selecting a data structure for a design problem (LRU cache)
voice.question: Suppose you need to implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Talk me through which data structures you'd combine and why, and how the eviction stays constant time.
voice.sample_strong_answer: An LRU cache needs two things at O(1): look up a value by key, and know which entry is least recently used so I can evict it. A hash map alone gives O(1) lookup but no recency ordering; a list gives ordering but O(n) to move an item to the front. So I combine a hash map with a doubly linked list. The map keys to nodes in the list; the list is ordered by recency, most-recently-used at the head, least at the tail. On get, I look the node up in the map in O(1), unlink it and move it to the head in O(1) because with a doubly linked list I have both neighbours' pointers. On put, if the key exists I update and move to head; if it's new I add at the head and insert into the map, and if I'm over capacity I evict the tail node and remove its key from the map, all O(1). The doubly linked list is essential because a singly linked list can't unlink a node in constant time without its predecessor. In Python I'd note collections.OrderedDict or functools.lru_cache gives this for free, using move_to_end, but the interview answer is the map-plus-linked-list design.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies the two required O(1) operations: keyed lookup and recency eviction
Explains why a single structure (map or list alone) is insufficient
Proposes hash map + doubly linked list combination
Explains head=MRU / tail=LRU ordering and O(1) move-to-head and evict-tail
Justifies doubly (not singly) linked list for O(1) unlink
Mentions OrderedDict/lru_cache as the practical Python route

voice.angle: Hash-based structures versus lists and choosing sets/dicts
voice.question: Talk me through how Python's dict and set achieve average O(1) lookup, and how you decide between a list, a set, and a dict for a given problem. When does the hash-based structure stop being the obvious win?
voice.sample_strong_answer: Dicts and sets are hash tables: they compute a hash of the key to find a bucket, so membership and lookup average O(1) instead of scanning. A list, by contrast, needs an O(n) linear scan for membership because it preserves order and allows duplicates and indexing. So I pick based on the operation that dominates. If I need fast membership tests or de-duplication, a set. If I need to map keys to values, a dict. If I need ordered, indexable, possibly duplicate data or I'm iterating in sequence, a list. The classic fix is replacing 'if x in some_list' inside a loop, which is accidental quadratic, with a set for constant-time checks. Where hash structures stop being the obvious win: keys must be hashable and effectively immutable, so you can't key on a list; there's memory overhead from the table; ordering by insertion is guaranteed for dict but sets are unordered; and if you need range queries, sorted iteration, or nearest-key lookups, a sorted structure or tree beats a hash table. Also worst-case lookup can degrade with pathological hashing, though CPython mitigates that. So the real question is which operations are hot and whether I need ordering or range semantics.
evaluation_criteria: Explains hashing to a bucket giving average O(1) versus O(n) list scan
Maps each structure to the operations it's best at
Cites the accidental-quadratic membership-in-list anti-pattern and its fix

Identifies when ordering, range queries, or sorted access favour other structures
Mentions memory overhead or worst-case degradation

voice.angle: The GIL and choosing between threading, multiprocessing, and asyncio
voice.question: Explain the Global Interpreter Lock and how it shapes your choice between threading, multiprocessing, and asyncio for concurrency in Python. Give me a decision framework with examples of when each wins.
voice.sample_strong_answer: In CPython the GIL is a mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so pure-Python CPU-bound work doesn't get real parallelism from threads. The key distinction is CPU-bound versus I/O-bound. For I/O-bound work, threads still help because a thread releases the GIL while it waits on the network or disk, so others run. asyncio also targets I/O but with cooperative single-threaded concurrency: one event loop multiplexes thousands of awaited operations with far less overhead than threads and no OS context switches, which is ideal for high-fan-out network work like calling many APIs or a server handling many sockets, provided the libraries are non-blocking. For CPU-bound work you need multiprocessing, which forks separate interpreter processes each with its own GIL, giving true parallelism at the cost of process overhead and inter-process communication and serialization. So my framework: CPU-bound and parallelizable, use multiprocessing or offload to native libraries that release the GIL like NumPy; I/O-bound with a manageable number of blocking calls, threads; I/O-bound at very high concurrency with async-native libraries, asyncio. I'd also note free-threaded builds are starting to relax the GIL, but the mental model still holds today.

Draws the CPU-bound vs I/O-bound distinction as the primary axis

voice.angle: Streaming top-k over data too large for memory
voice.question: You need the top K most frequent items from a stream that's far too large to hold in memory, and it keeps arriving. Walk me through your algorithmic approach, the data structures, and the accuracy-versus-resources trade-offs.
voice.sample_strong_answer: First I separate two sub-problems: counting frequencies, and maintaining the top K. If the set of distinct keys fits in memory even though the stream doesn't, I keep a hash map of counts and a min-heap of size K keyed by count. I scan once; for each item I bump its count, and if it qualifies I push or replace the heap root, so the heap always holds the current top K in O(log K) per update and O(1) to read. That's exact and single-pass. The hard case is when even the distinct keys don't fit. Then I go probabilistic: a Count-Min Sketch gives approximate counts in fixed sub-linear memory by hashing into several counter arrays and taking the min, trading a bounded overestimate for huge memory savings, and I pair it with a small heap of candidate heavy hitters. Algorithms like Space-Saving or Lossy Counting are purpose-built for heavy hitters with tight error bounds. The trade-offs are exactness versus memory: sketches can overcount rare items and miss borderline ones, and error scales with how skewed the distribution is. For an unbounded live stream I'd also add windowing or decay so recent data dominates, and if it's distributed I'd compute partial top-K per shard and merge, accepting that merging approximate counts loosens guarantees.
evaluation_criteria: Separates frequency counting from top-K maintenance
Gives the exact solution: hash-map counts + size-K min-heap with O(log K) updates
Recognises the regime where distinct keys exceed memory

Addresses the streaming/unbounded nature via windowing or decay

voice.angle: Purpose and value of automated tests
voice.question: Explain why you write automated tests and what a good unit test gives you. What distinguishes a useful test from one that just inflates coverage?
voice.sample_strong_answer: Automated tests exist to catch regressions cheaply and to let me change code with confidence. A good unit test pins down the behaviour of a small piece of code in isolation, runs fast and deterministically, and fails clearly when the behaviour breaks, so I get a fast feedback loop instead of finding bugs in production. Beyond catching bugs, tests document intent, they show how a function is meant to be used, and they pressure the design toward small, decoupled units, because hard-to-test code is usually badly coupled. A useful test asserts on meaningful behaviour and covers edge cases and error paths, not just the happy path, uses realistic inputs, and has a name that says what it verifies. A low-value test just calls the code to bump the coverage number, asserts nothing important or asserts on implementation details so it breaks on every refactor, or is flaky because it depends on time, network, or ordering. Coverage tells you what ran, not what was verified, so I treat it as a guardrail, not a goal. I'd add that the pyramid matters: lots of fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests, so the suite stays fast and trustworthy.

Describes qualities of a good unit test (isolated, fast, deterministic, clear failure)
Notes tests document intent and improve design/testability
Distinguishes behaviour-focused assertions from coverage-only tests
Warns against brittle/implementation-coupled and flaky tests
Frames coverage as a guardrail not a goal, or mentions the test pyramid

voice.angle: Systematic debugging of an intermittent production issue
voice.question: You're facing an intermittent bug that only shows up in production under load and never reproduces locally. Walk me through your systematic debugging methodology end to end, how you form and test hypotheses, and how you avoid making it worse.
voice.sample_strong_answer: I treat it as science, not guesswork. First, make it observable: gather evidence from logs, metrics, traces, and error rates, and nail down what exactly happens, how often, and under what conditions, so I have a precise problem statement instead of a vibe. Intermittent-under-load almost always points at concurrency, resource exhaustion, or a data-dependent edge case, race conditions, connection-pool or memory limits, timeouts, a rare input, or an external dependency degrading. Next I try to shrink the reproduction: correlate incidents with a deploy, a traffic pattern, a specific tenant or payload; add targeted structured logging or distributed tracing around the suspect path; and try to reproduce with a load test that mimics the concurrency, since 'works locally' usually means local load is too gentle. Then I form one hypothesis at a time and test it, changing a single variable, because if I change five things I learn nothing. To avoid making it worse, I work in a safe way: feature flags, canary or shadow traffic, and reversible changes, and I add instrumentation before I add fixes. I keep a written timeline so the team shares state. Once I have a suspected root cause I confirm it by reproducing on demand, fix it, and, critically, add a regression test and an alert so it can't silently return. The discipline is evidence first, one hypothesis at a time, reversible changes, and close the loop with a test.

Enumerates load-specific likely causes (races, resource exhaustion, timeouts, rare data, flaky dependency)
Describes narrowing the reproduction via correlation, tracing, and realistic load testing
Tests one hypothesis at a time, changing a single variable
Uses safe/reversible mechanisms (flags, canary, shadow) to avoid worsening prod
Closes the loop with a regression test and monitoring/alerting
Emphasises confirming root cause before declaring victory

voice.angle: Git workflow, and merge versus rebase
voice.question: Describe a Git branching workflow you'd use on a team, and explain the difference between merge and rebase. When would you rebase, when would you merge, and what's the golden rule you never break?
voice.sample_strong_answer: On a team I'd use short-lived feature branches off main with pull requests, CI on every branch, and small frequent merges to avoid long-lived divergence. On merge versus rebase: merging integrates two branches by creating a merge commit that ties both histories together, preserving exactly what happened, including the branching. Rebase replays my branch's commits on top of the latest main, producing a linear history as if I'd started from the current tip, but it rewrites commit hashes because it creates new commits. I rebase locally to keep my feature branch current and to tidy my own commits before opening or updating a PR, because linear history is easier to read and bisect. I merge when integrating a finished feature into main, often a squash or a merge commit, so the shared history is stable. The golden rule is never rebase or force-push a branch other people have already pulled, because rewriting shared history breaks everyone's copy and causes duplicated commits and painful conflicts. So: rebase private history, merge public history. I'd also mention resolving conflicts carefully and keeping commits atomic so bisect and review stay useful.
evaluation_criteria: Describes a coherent branching model (short-lived branches, PRs, CI)
Correctly contrasts merge (merge commit, preserves history) with rebase (linear, rewrites commits)
States rebase for private/local cleanup and staying current
States merge for integrating into shared branches
Articulates the golden rule: don't rebase/force-push shared history
Mentions atomic commits, conflict handling, or bisect readability

voice.angle: Dependency management, virtual environments, and reproducible builds
voice.question: Explain how you manage Python dependencies for a project so builds are reproducible. Cover virtual environments, pinning, the difference between direct and transitive dependencies, and lock files.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Reproducibility means anyone, and CI, gets the exact same environment. First, isolation: each project gets its own virtual environment so its dependencies don't collide with the system or other projects. Second, I separate what I declare from what actually gets installed. My direct dependencies, the ones my code imports, I specify with sensible version constraints in something like pyproject.toml. But those pull in transitive dependencies, and if I only pin the direct ones, a transitive package can silently update and break me. So the key is a lock file that records the fully resolved graph with exact pinned versions and ideally hashes, produced by a resolver like pip-tools, Poetry, or uv. CI and production install from the lock file, so the build is deterministic; I only re-resolve deliberately when I intend to upgrade, then review the diff and run tests. I'd also separate dev dependencies from runtime ones, use hashes to defend against tampering, and be mindful of Python-version and platform differences in the lock. The anti-pattern is a hand-maintained requirements file with loose or no pins, which gives you 'works on my machine' drift. So: isolate, declare with constraints, lock the full resolved set, and install from the lock.
evaluation_criteria: Explains virtual-environment isolation per project
Distinguishes direct from transitive dependencies
Explains pinning and why loose/unpinned deps cause drift
Describes lock files capturing the fully resolved graph with exact versions/hashes
Separates the declared-vs-installed and dev-vs-runtime concerns
Names real tooling (pip-tools/Poetry/uv) and the deliberate-upgrade flow

Signature: def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
code.reference_solution:
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    c = Counter(nums)
    items = sorted(c.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))
    return [v for v, _ in items[:k]]

voice.angle: Indexing and the N+1 query problem
voice.question: Explain how database indexes speed up queries and what they cost, and separately describe the N+1 query problem and how you'd fix it. How do these two topics relate to a slow endpoint?
voice.sample_strong_answer: An index is a separate sorted data structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows matching a predicate without scanning the whole table, turning an O(n) scan into roughly O(log n) lookup, and it also speeds ordering and range queries on the indexed columns. The cost is that every index adds storage and slows writes, because inserts, updates, and deletes must maintain it, so you index the columns you actually filter, join, or sort on, not everything. The N+1 problem is different: it's an application pattern where you run one query to fetch a list of parent rows, then fire a separate query per row to fetch related data, so N items cost N+1 round trips. It's brutal because each round trip has latency, so an endpoint that looks fine on ten rows crawls on a thousand. The fix is to fetch related data in bulk: a JOIN, or an eager-load / IN-clause that pulls all children in one query, which ORMs expose as eager loading or select-in loading. They relate because a slow endpoint is often both, an unindexed filter doing full scans and an ORM quietly issuing N+1 queries. My approach is to look at the query plan with EXPLAIN, add the missing index, and batch the related fetches, then measure again. The theme is fewer round trips and index-backed lookups.

States the write/storage cost and 'index what you query' guidance
Correctly defines N+1 as 1 query plus one-per-row follow-ups
Explains why round-trip latency makes N+1 scale badly
Gives the fix: joins/eager loading/batched IN queries
Mentions using EXPLAIN/query plans to diagnose

voice.angle: Relational versus NoSQL and when to choose each
voice.question: Explain how you decide between a relational SQL database and a NoSQL store for a new service. What properties drive the choice, and what do you give up in each direction?
voice.sample_strong_answer: I start from the data and the access patterns, not fashion. Relational databases give you a fixed schema, rich joins, and strong ACID transactions, so they shine when data is highly relational, when you need multi-row consistency like financial or inventory operations, and when query patterns are varied or evolving, because SQL lets you ask new questions without redesigning storage. The cost is that horizontal scaling and very high write throughput are harder, and rigid schemas need migrations. NoSQL is an umbrella: document stores, key-value, wide-column, and graph, each optimised differently. They typically trade joins and sometimes strong consistency for flexible schemas, high write scale, and predictable low-latency access when you query by a known key. So a document store fits denormalised, self-contained documents with known access paths; key-value fits caches and sessions; wide-column fits massive write-heavy time series; graph fits highly connected traversal queries. The trade-off is you must model around your queries up front and often accept eventual consistency and data duplication. My rule of thumb: default to relational unless a specific requirement, extreme scale, a truly schemaless shape, or a specialised access pattern, justifies NoSQL, and remember you can combine them, relational as the system of record with a cache or search index alongside. The deciding factors are consistency needs, query shape, scale, and schema volatility.

Correctly attributes schema/joins/ACID strengths to relational
Notes relational scaling/migration costs
Treats NoSQL as multiple families with different optimisations
Explains the trade-offs: flexible schema/scale versus joins and consistency
Gives a sensible default (relational unless justified) and polyglot option

voice.angle: Transactions, isolation levels, and race conditions
voice.question: Explain database transactions and isolation levels, and how they prevent race conditions like two users updating the same balance concurrently. Walk through the anomalies each isolation level allows and how you'd choose, including optimistic versus pessimistic locking.
voice.sample_strong_answer: A transaction groups operations so they're atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable, all-or-nothing and, ideally, as if run alone. Isolation level controls how much concurrent transactions can see each other, trading correctness for concurrency. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, seeing another transaction's uncommitted data. Read Committed prevents that but allows non-repeatable reads, the same row read twice can differ. Repeatable Read stabilises rows you've read but can still allow phantoms, new rows matching your query appearing, and depending on the engine, write skew. Serializable is the strongest, results equivalent to some serial order, preventing all these, at the cost of more aborts or blocking. The classic balance race is a lost update: two transactions read the same balance, both add to it, and the second overwrites the first. Read Committed does not stop this by itself. Two fixes: pessimistic locking, SELECT FOR UPDATE, which locks the row so the second transaction waits, simple and safe under high contention; or optimistic concurrency, read a version, and on write assert the version hasn't changed, retrying on conflict, which is cheaper when conflicts are rare. You can also push the arithmetic into the database, UPDATE balance = balance - amount with a guard, so the DB serialises it. So I choose isolation and locking by contention and correctness needs: Serializable or explicit locks for money, lighter levels where anomalies are tolerable.

voice.angle: Why and when to scale features
voice.question: Explain aloud why feature scaling or normalisation matters in machine learning, and name a couple of model types where it's important versus where it doesn't matter. Keep it practical.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Feature scaling puts features onto comparable ranges, typically by standardising to zero mean and unit variance, or min-max scaling to a fixed range. It matters whenever a model treats feature magnitudes as meaningful. Distance-based methods like k-nearest neighbours, k-means, and RBF-kernel SVMs are dominated by whichever feature has the largest numeric range, so an unscaled feature in thousands drowns out one in fractions. Gradient-based models, linear and logistic regression and neural networks, converge faster and more stably when inputs are scaled because the loss surface becomes better conditioned, and any model with L1 or L2 regularisation needs scaling so the penalty is applied fairly across features. On the other hand, tree-based models, decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting, are invariant to monotonic rescaling because they split on thresholds, so scaling doesn't change their results. The one operational rule I always follow is to fit the scaler on the training data only and apply those same parameters to validation and test, ideally inside a pipeline, otherwise you leak information from the test set and get optimistic results.
evaluation_criteria: Explains scaling makes feature ranges comparable (standardisation or min-max)
Identifies distance-based models as scaling-sensitive
Notes gradient-based models converge better when scaled
Links regularisation penalties to the need for scaling
States tree-based models are scale-invariant
Mentions fitting the scaler on training data only to avoid leakage

common_pitfalls: Claiming all models need scaling, including trees

voice.question: Explain aloud the options for encoding a high-cardinality categorical feature, something like a zip code or product ID with thousands of levels. Compare the main approaches and say how you'd choose.
voice.sample_strong_answer: One-hot encoding is fine for low cardinality but explodes into thousands of sparse columns for something like zip code, which bloats memory, slows training, and dilutes signal, so I look at alternatives. The first is target or mean encoding, where I replace each category with a smoothed statistic of the target for that category, blended toward the global mean so rare levels don't overfit; it's compact and powerful but leaks the target if done naively, so it must be computed with cross-fold or out-of-fold schemes and fit only on training data. Frequency or count encoding replaces the level with how often it appears, which is cheap and sometimes informative. Hashing the feature into a fixed number of buckets bounds dimensionality and handles unseen categories, at the cost of collisions and lost interpretability. Learned embeddings, mapping each category to a dense trainable vector, are excellent when I have a neural net and lots of data, and they capture similarity between categories. There's also grouping rare levels into an 'other' bucket. For tree models like LightGBM or CatBoost I'd often lean on their native categorical handling, and CatBoost's ordered target encoding is specifically designed to avoid leakage. So my choice depends on cardinality, model type, data size, and leakage risk: for a boosted-tree tabular model with thousands of levels I'd typically use ordered target encoding or native handling; for a deep model I'd use embeddings; and I'd always validate the encoding inside the cross-validation loop, never on the full dataset.

Describes target/mean encoding with smoothing and its leakage risk

code.title: Collect paginated records
code.prompt:
Implement `collect_pages(pages)`.

`pages` is a dictionary mapping cursor values to page dictionaries with `items` and `next_cursor`.
Start at cursor `"START"`, follow `next_cursor`, and return all items in order.
Raise `ValueError` if a cursor repeats, preventing an infinite loop.
code.reference_solution:
def collect_pages(pages):
    cursor = "START"
    seen = set()
    out = []
    while cursor is not None:
        if cursor in seen:
            raise ValueError("cursor loop")
        seen.add(cursor)
        page = pages[cursor]
        out.extend(page["items"])
        cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
    return out

code.title: Flag IQR outliers
code.prompt:
Implement `iqr_outlier_mask(values)`.

Return a boolean list using the 1.5×IQR rule.
For this task, quartiles are computed by sorting and taking the median of the lower and upper halves;
when the length is odd, exclude the overall median from both halves.
For fewer than four values, return all `False`.
code.reference_solution:
def iqr_outlier_mask(values):
    n = len(values)
    if n < 4:
        return [False] * n
    s = sorted(values)
    def median(xs):
        m = len(xs)
        mid = m // 2
        return xs[mid] if m % 2 else (xs[mid-1] + xs[mid]) / 2
    mid = n // 2
    lower = s[:mid]
    upper = s[mid+1:] if n % 2 else s[mid:]
    q1, q3 = median(lower), median(upper)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    return [v < lo or v > hi for v in values]

code.title: Reproducible train/test split indices
code.prompt: Produce a reproducible train/test split of index positions 0..n-1. Build the list of indices, shuffle it with random.Random(seed).shuffle, then take the first int(n * test_ratio) shuffled indices as the test set and the remainder as the train set. Return [train, test] where each is a list of indices in shuffled order. Use exactly random.Random(seed) so results are deterministic. Signature: def train_test_split_indices(n, test_ratio, seed):
code.reference_solution:
def train_test_split_indices(n, test_ratio, seed):
    import random
    idx = list(range(n))
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    rng.shuffle(idx)
    t = int(n * test_ratio)
    test = idx[:t]
    train = idx[t:]
    return [train, test]

code.title: Z-score standardization
code.prompt: Standardize a feature column to zero mean and unit variance using z = (x - mean) / std, where std is the population standard deviation (divide by N, not N-1). Return a new list, each value rounded to 6 decimals. If the standard deviation is 0 (constant column), return a list of 0.0. An empty input returns an empty list. Signature: def standardize(xs):
code.reference_solution:
def standardize(xs):
    import math
    n = len(xs)
    if n == 0:
        return []
    mean = sum(xs) / n
    var = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in xs) / n
    sd = math.sqrt(var)
    if sd == 0:
        return [0.0] * n
    return [round((x - mean) / sd, 6) for x in xs]

voice.angle: Choosing a model family for the problem
voice.question: A stakeholder gives you a new predictive problem. Explain aloud how you'd decide which model family to start with. What properties of the data and the task drive that choice?
voice.sample_strong_answer: I let the data and constraints choose the family rather than my favourite algorithm. First, the data modality: for structured tabular data, gradient-boosted trees are my default strong choice; for images I reach for CNNs or vision transformers; for text, transformer-based language models; for sequences or time series, models that respect temporal structure. Second, dataset size: with only a few thousand rows I favour simpler, well-regularised models or classical ML that won't overfit, whereas deep learning needs large data or transfer learning to shine. Third, the nature of the relationship: if it's plausibly linear a linear or logistic model may suffice and is interpretable; if there are strong non-linear interactions, trees or nets fit better. Fourth, the requirements around interpretability, latency, and deployment, a regulated setting may demand a transparent model like logistic regression or a small tree, while a low-latency service constrains model size. Fifth, feature types and missingness, since tree ensembles handle mixed types and missing values gracefully. And I weigh label quality and cost of errors, which drive the metric and thus the model too. Practically, I start with a simple baseline and a strong tabular default like LightGBM, measure with proper cross-validation, and only escalate to heavier models if the data volume and the performance gap justify the extra complexity and maintenance cost.

voice.question: Explain aloud how a decision tree decides where to split, and how it uses those splits to make a prediction. Keep it intuitive, as if explaining to a junior analyst.
voice.sample_strong_answer: A decision tree learns a set of if-then rules by recursively partitioning the feature space. At each node it looks at every feature and every candidate threshold and picks the split that best separates the data according to an impurity measure. For classification that's usually Gini impurity or entropy/information gain, and for regression it's the reduction in variance or mean squared error. It greedily chooses the split that most reduces impurity, then repeats the process on each resulting child node. It keeps splitting until a stopping condition, like maximum depth, a minimum number of samples per leaf, or no further impurity reduction. To predict, you drop a new example in at the root and follow the branches according to its feature values until you land in a leaf; the prediction is the majority class in that leaf for classification, or the average target value for regression. Trees are attractive because they're interpretable, handle mixed feature types, need no scaling, and capture non-linear interactions, but a single deep tree overfits easily, which is why we prune them or, more commonly, combine many trees into ensembles like random forests or gradient boosting.

voice.question: Explain aloud the bias-variance trade-off in your own words. What do bias and variance each mean, and how do they relate to model complexity and generalisation?
voice.sample_strong_answer: The bias-variance trade-off decomposes a model's expected error on unseen data into three parts: bias, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is error from the model being too simple to capture the true relationship, it makes systematically wrong assumptions, so it underfits and does poorly on both training and test data. Variance is error from the model being too sensitive to the particular training sample, it fits noise, so it does great on training data but poorly on new data, that's overfitting. There's a tension because reducing one tends to raise the other: as I increase model complexity, more parameters, deeper trees, higher polynomial degree, bias falls but variance rises. A very simple model, like predicting the mean, has high bias and low variance; a very flexible model, like a deep unpruned tree, has low bias and high variance. Generalisation error is minimised somewhere in the middle where their sum is smallest, and my job is to find that sweet spot, using tools like regularisation, cross-validation, more data, or ensembling. More data mainly reduces variance, and regularisation trades a bit more bias for a lot less variance. The intuition I keep is: high train error means bias, a big gap between train and test error means variance.

voice.question: Compare aloud bagging and boosting as ensemble strategies. Explain how each one reduces error, and what kinds of base learners and problems each is suited to.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Both bagging and boosting combine many weak-ish models into a stronger one, but they attack different parts of the error. Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, trains many models in parallel on bootstrap resamples of the data and averages their predictions, or votes for classification. Because the models are trained independently on slightly different data and, in random forests, random feature subsets, their errors are partly decorrelated, so averaging mainly reduces variance without much affecting bias. That's why bagging pairs well with high-variance, low-bias learners like deep unpruned trees. It's robust to overfitting, parallelisable, and forgiving of hyperparameters. Boosting instead trains models sequentially, where each new model focuses on the examples the current ensemble gets wrong, either by reweighting them as in AdaBoost or by fitting the residual gradient as in gradient boosting. This primarily reduces bias, turning weak learners like shallow trees into a strong committee, and it usually reaches higher accuracy than bagging on tabular data. The trade-off is that boosting is sequential so harder to parallelise, and because it keeps fitting to residuals it can overfit noise if you use too many rounds or too high a learning rate, so it needs early stopping and careful tuning. Rule of thumb: bagging or random forests when you want a robust, low-tuning baseline; gradient boosting like XGBoost, LightGBM or CatBoost when you want to squeeze out maximum accuracy and can afford tuning.

voice.question: Compare aloud L1 and L2 regularisation. Explain how each affects the model's weights, why L1 produces sparsity, and when you'd prefer one over the other.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Both add a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss to discourage overfitting, but the shape of the penalty differs. L2, ridge, penalises the sum of squared weights, so it shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero but rarely exactly to zero; it handles correlated features gracefully by spreading weight among them and gives a stable, well-conditioned solution. L1, lasso, penalises the sum of absolute weights, and its key property is that it drives some coefficients exactly to zero, performing automatic feature selection and yielding a sparse, interpretable model. The geometric reason is that the L1 constraint region is a diamond with sharp corners on the axes, so the loss contours tend to touch it at a corner where some weights are zero, whereas the L2 region is a smooth circle that's touched off-axis, giving small but nonzero weights. I prefer L1 when I suspect many features are irrelevant and want a compact, selectable model; I prefer L2 when features are correlated or I want stable shrinkage without discarding variables. Elastic net combines both with a mix parameter and is often the safe default with correlated groups of features, since pure L1 can arbitrarily pick one of a correlated group and drop the rest. The regularisation strength is a hyperparameter I tune by cross-validation, and I scale features first so the penalty is applied fairly.

voice.angle: Random forest vs gradient boosting trade-offs
voice.question: A colleague asks whether to use a random forest or a gradient-boosted tree model for a new tabular problem. Talk through aloud how you would decide, covering accuracy, tuning burden, overfitting behaviour, training and inference cost, and any data conditions that push you one way or the other.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Both are tree ensembles but with different bias-variance dynamics, so my choice depends on constraints, not just accuracy. Random forests average many deep, decorrelated trees, so they mainly cut variance; they're remarkably robust out of the box, need little tuning, are trivially parallelisable, resist overfitting as you add trees, and give a free out-of-bag error estimate. Their ceiling on accuracy is usually a bit lower and their models can be large and slow at inference because every tree is deep. Gradient boosting builds shallow trees sequentially to reduce bias and typically wins on tabular accuracy, especially modern implementations like LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost, which also handle categorical features and missing values well and can be fast at inference with shallow trees. The cost is that boosting is sensitive to hyperparameters, learning rate, number of rounds, depth, regularisation, and it will overfit if you over-train, so it needs a validation set and early stopping, and training is sequential. So my decision: if I need a strong, low-effort baseline fast, or the team can't invest in tuning, I reach for a random forest. If accuracy is the priority and I can afford tuning and monitoring, I go gradient boosting with early stopping. Data conditions matter too: with lots of label noise or very small data, the forest's robustness is safer; with strong signal and a need to extract every point of performance, boosting wins. And whichever I pick, I'd benchmark both against a simple baseline and compare on a proper cross-validated metric before committing, since on many tabular problems the gap is small and other factors, latency, interpretability, maintenance, decide it.

voice.question: Explain aloud how the optimal amount of regularisation interacts with the size of your training set and the signal-to-noise ratio of the problem. Why might the regularisation strength you tuned on a small dataset be wrong once you have ten times more data?
voice.sample_strong_answer: Regularisation is a lever on the bias-variance trade-off: it adds bias to cut variance. How much variance there is to cut depends heavily on data size and noise. With a small dataset, the model has lots of variance because it can easily fit sampling noise, so strong regularisation pays off, accepting more bias to rein in that variance. As I add more data, variance naturally falls because the estimates are better constrained by evidence, so the marginal benefit of regularisation shrinks and the optimal strength decreases; the model can now afford to be more flexible and fit finer structure without overfitting. That's why a penalty tuned on a small sample is often too strong for a much larger one, it would now underfit, leaving signal on the table. Signal-to-noise ratio matters too: in a noisy problem, more regularisation is warranted because much of what a flexible model would fit is noise; in a clean, high-signal problem, less regularisation is better. So the strength isn't a fixed property of the problem, it depends on how much data and how much noise, and it must be re-tuned when the data volume changes materially. Practically, I re-run cross-validated tuning after a big data increase, expect the optimal penalty to drop, and I watch the learning curve: if train and validation error have converged and both are high, I'm regularising or under-modelling too much; if there's still a wide gap, I need more regularisation or more data. This is also why the best regularisation strength interacts with model capacity, you tune them together, not in isolation.

voice.angle: What calibration means and why it matters
voice.question: Explain aloud what it means for a classifier's predicted probabilities to be well calibrated, why calibration can matter more than accuracy in some applications, and how you'd assess and improve it.
voice.sample_strong_answer: A classifier is well calibrated when its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, among all cases it says are 70 percent likely to be positive, about 70 percent actually are. That's distinct from discrimination or accuracy, which is about ranking or getting the label right; a model can rank well, high AUC, yet be badly calibrated, systematically over- or under-confident. Calibration matters whenever the probability itself is used, not just the top class: expected-value decisions like whether to approve a loan or intervene medically, thresholding against a cost, risk scoring, or feeding probabilities into a downstream optimisation. There an overconfident 0.9 that's really 0.6 leads to bad decisions even if the ranking is fine. I assess calibration with a reliability diagram, binning predictions and plotting predicted versus actual frequency, and summarise it with the Expected Calibration Error or Brier score, which also captures sharpness. Common culprits: models like SVMs or naive Bayes produce distorted scores, and modern neural nets tend to be overconfident. To improve it I fit a post-hoc calibrator on a held-out set, Platt scaling, a logistic fit, or isotonic regression, which is more flexible but needs more data, or temperature scaling for neural nets, which rescales logits with a single parameter and preserves accuracy. Crucially I fit the calibrator on separate data from training to avoid leakage, and I recheck calibration after any threshold or distribution change, since drift can decalibrate a previously good model.
evaluation_criteria: Defines calibration as predicted probabilities matching observed frequencies
Distinguishes calibration from discrimination/accuracy (a model can rank well but be miscalibrated)
Explains when calibration matters (probability used for decisions/expected value/risk)
Describes assessment (reliability diagram, ECE, Brier score)
Names calibration methods (Platt/logistic, isotonic, temperature scaling)
Notes fitting the calibrator on held-out data and rechecking after drift

voice.angle: Why cross-validation over a single split
voice.question: Explain aloud what k-fold cross-validation is and why you'd use it instead of a single train-test split. What does it buy you, and what are its costs?
voice.sample_strong_answer: K-fold cross-validation splits the data into k equal folds, then trains k times, each time holding out a different fold for validation and training on the other k-1, and averages the metric across the k runs. Compared with a single train-test split it does two things. First, it gives a more reliable, lower-variance estimate of generalisation performance, because a single split can be lucky or unlucky depending on which rows happen to land in the test set, especially with limited data; averaging over folds reduces that dependence and lets me report a mean with a spread. Second, every example gets used for both training and validation across the folds, so I make efficient use of scarce data. It's also the right vehicle for hyperparameter tuning and model comparison, because I can compare average scores and their variability rather than a single noisy number. The costs are that it's k times more compute, since I train k models, and it can be misused, I must keep a truly held-out test set for the final estimate, apply all preprocessing inside each fold to avoid leakage, and use the right variant, stratified k-fold for imbalanced classification to preserve class ratios, grouped k-fold when rows share an entity, and time-series splits for temporal data where random folds would leak the future. For very large datasets a single large split can be enough since variance is already low, so cross-validation is most valuable when data is limited.

voice.question: For a highly imbalanced classification problem, say fraud at one percent, explain aloud why accuracy is a poor metric and which metrics you'd use instead. Justify your choice in terms of the business cost of errors.
voice.sample_strong_answer: With one percent positives, a model that predicts 'not fraud' for everything scores 99 percent accuracy while catching zero fraud, so accuracy is useless, it's dominated by the majority class and rewards ignoring the rare class I actually care about. Instead I focus on the positive class. Precision is the fraction of flagged cases that are truly fraud, and recall is the fraction of actual fraud I catch; there's a trade-off between them governed by the decision threshold. Which matters more depends on error costs: missing fraud, a false negative, might cost the chargeback, while a false alarm, a false positive, costs an investigation and customer friction, so I'd quantify those and often optimise a cost-weighted objective or an F-beta score that weights recall and precision according to that cost. For threshold-independent comparison I use the precision-recall curve and its area, which is far more informative than ROC-AUC under heavy imbalance because ROC can look deceptively good when true negatives dominate. I'd also look at recall at a fixed precision or precision at a fixed alert budget, since operationally the fraud team can only review so many cases a day. And because the raw score threshold drives everything, I'd choose it deliberately from the precision-recall trade-off to hit the business's tolerance, rather than defaulting to 0.5. In short: drop accuracy, reason about false-positive versus false-negative costs, and pick precision, recall, F-beta, and PR-AUC accordingly.

voice.angle: Deciding if one model truly beats another
voice.question: You have two models and model B scores half a point higher than model A on your test metric. Explain aloud how you'd decide whether B is genuinely better, rather than better by chance. What would you check?
voice.sample_strong_answer: A half-point difference on a single test set could easily be noise, so I wouldn't declare a winner from one number. First I'd quantify uncertainty. I'd compare the two models across the same cross-validation folds and look at the distribution of the metric, not just the mean, ideally paired per fold so I control for which data each was evaluated on. Bootstrapping the test set to get confidence intervals on each score and on their difference tells me whether the gap's interval excludes zero. For a more formal check I might use a paired test, like a paired t-test or Wilcoxon across folds, or McNemar's test on the paired classification errors, while being mindful that fold scores aren't fully independent, so I treat p-values as rough guidance. Crucially, both models must be evaluated on identical splits and the comparison metric must be the one that matters. Then I'd go beyond the aggregate: I'd slice performance by important segments to see if B's gain is uniform or concentrated, check calibration and the error types, and weigh practical factors, latency, size, complexity, interpretability, maintenance cost, and stability across time. And I'd make sure I'm not overfitting the test set from repeated comparisons. If B's improvement is within the noise band or comes with much higher cost, I'd keep the simpler model A; I only switch when the gain is both statistically credible and practically meaningful.

Uses cross-validation across identical folds and looks at the metric distribution/variance

voice.angle: Splitting for time-series and grouped data
voice.question: Explain aloud why standard random k-fold cross-validation can be dangerously misleading for time-series or grouped data, and describe the correct splitting strategies for each case and how they mirror production.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Random k-fold assumes rows are independent and exchangeable, but time-series and grouped data violate that, so it leaks and gives optimistic scores that collapse in production. For time series, random folds put future observations in the training set and past ones in validation, so the model effectively sees the future, and autocorrelation means neighbouring points are near-duplicates. The correct approach respects temporal order: forward-chaining or expanding-window validation, where I always train on the past and validate on a later block, rolling forward, optionally with a gap or embargo between train and validation to avoid look-ahead from lagged features. That mirrors production, where I only ever have the past to predict the future, and it also lets me see if performance drifts over time. For grouped data, where many rows belong to the same entity, patient, user, customer, session, random folds put the same entity in both train and validation, so the model memorises entity-specific quirks and looks better than it will on genuinely new entities. The fix is grouped k-fold, or leave-one-group-out, so all rows of an entity stay together on one side of the split, which mirrors production if we'll predict on unseen entities. You can combine them, grouped and time-based, when data is both temporal and clustered. The unifying principle is that the split must reproduce the real prediction scenario: what will actually be known, and how novel the test cases will be, at inference time. I also keep a final out-of-time test period untouched, and I'd rather a slightly pessimistic honest estimate than an optimistic leaked one.

voice.question: You're deploying a model into an environment where the data distribution will drift over time, user behaviour, seasonality, and upstream changes all shift. Explain aloud how you would design an evaluation and monitoring strategy that stays trustworthy under a shifting distribution, and how you'd distinguish genuine model degradation from noise.
voice.sample_strong_answer: Under drift, a fixed test set from the past stops representing production, so my evaluation has to be continuous and time-aware rather than a one-off. First, offline I validate with out-of-time splits and backtesting across multiple historical periods, so I know how the model holds up across regime changes, not just on a random split. In production I monitor on two levels. Input monitoring watches for covariate shift, tracking feature distributions and the prediction distribution with drift measures like population stability index or KL divergence, and data-quality checks, because I get these signals immediately, before labels arrive. Outcome monitoring watches actual performance once labels land, but labels are often delayed, so I design a labelling pipeline, sometimes with delayed ground truth, sometimes with human review of a sample, sometimes proxy metrics, and I track the metric on rolling windows and by segment, since drift often hits one cohort first. To separate real degradation from noise I don't react to a single dip: I use control-chart or sequential-test thinking, confidence intervals and rolling baselines, and require a change that's both statistically significant given the sample size and sustained, not a one-day blip, ideally corroborated by input drift so I understand the mechanism. I'd distinguish covariate shift, where inputs move but the input-output relationship holds and recalibration or reweighting may suffice, from concept drift, where the relationship itself changes and I need retraining on fresh data. I'd hold out a rolling recent slice as an always-fresh evaluation set, keep a champion-challenger or shadow deployment so a candidate is judged on current data before switching, set alert thresholds tied to business impact, and plan a retraining and rollback cadence. The core principle is that evaluation must move with the distribution and decisions must clear both a significance bar and a persistence bar before I act.

Uses out-of-time backtesting across multiple periods offline

Separates noise from real degradation via significance + persistence (control charts, CIs, sustained change)
Distinguishes covariate shift (recalibrate/reweight) from concept drift (retrain)
Adds operational design: rolling fresh eval set, champion-challenger/shadow, alert thresholds, retrain/rollback cadence

code.title: k-NN classification prediction
code.prompt: Implement a single k-NN classification prediction. Given train (a list of feature vectors), labels (the label for each training point), a query feature vector, and integer k, find the k training points with the smallest Euclidean distance to the query and return the majority-vote label. Break ties (in vote counts) by choosing the smallest label value. When distances tie for the k-th slot, prefer the point that appears earlier in train. Signature: def euclidean_knn_predict(train, labels, query, k):
code.reference_solution:
def euclidean_knn_predict(train, labels, query, k):
    import math
    from collections import Counter
    dists = []
    for i, pt in enumerate(train):
        d = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(pt, query)))
        dists.append((d, i, labels[i]))
    dists.sort(key=lambda t: (t[0], t[1]))
    nearest = [lbl for _, _, lbl in dists[:k]]
    counts = Counter(nearest)
    top = max(counts.values())
    return min(l for l in counts if counts[l] == top)

code.title: k-fold cross-validation indices
code.prompt: Generate k-fold cross-validation splits over indices 0..n-1 WITHOUT shuffling. Fold sizes are as even as possible: the first (n mod k) folds get one extra element. Validation indices for each fold are a contiguous block; the training indices are all other indices in ascending order. Return a list of k folds, each a pair [train, val]. Raise ValueError if k < 2 or k > n. Signature: def kfold_indices(n, k):
code.reference_solution:
def kfold_indices(n, k):
    if k < 2 or k > n:
        raise ValueError('invalid k')
    indices = list(range(n))
    fold_sizes = [n // k + (1 if i < n % k else 0) for i in range(k)]
    folds = []
    cur = 0
    for fs in fold_sizes:
        val = indices[cur:cur + fs]
        train = indices[:cur] + indices[cur + fs:]
        folds.append([train, val])
        cur += fs
    return folds

code.title: Macro-averaged precision, recall & F1
code.prompt: Given y_true, y_pred (equal-length label lists) and labels (ordered class list), compute the MACRO-averaged precision, recall and F1 score. For each class c: precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R); any of these is 0.0 when its denominator is 0. Macro-average = unweighted mean across the classes in labels. Return the list [macro_precision, macro_recall, macro_f1], each rounded to 6 decimals. Signature: def precision_recall_f1(y_true, y_pred, labels):
code.reference_solution:
def precision_recall_f1(y_true, y_pred, labels):
    ps, rs, fs = [], [], []
    for c in labels:
        tp = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t == c and p == c)
        fp = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t != c and p == c)
        fn = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t == c and p != c)
        prec = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) else 0.0
        rec = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) else 0.0
        f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) if (prec + rec) else 0.0
        ps.append(prec); rs.append(rec); fs.append(f1)
    k = len(labels)
    return [round(sum(ps) / k, 6), round(sum(rs) / k, 6), round(sum(fs) / k, 6)]

code.title: ROC curve points from scores
code.prompt: Given y_true (binary labels 0/1) and scores (predicted positive-class scores), compute the points of the ROC curve. Sort samples by score descending; sweeping the threshold from +infinity downward, start at (0.0, 0.0) and, after including each group of samples that share the same score, emit the point [FPR, TPR] where FPR = FP / N (N = number of true negatives) and TPR = TP / P (P = number of true positives). Ties in score must be consumed together before emitting a point. Round each coordinate to 6 decimals. Assume at least one positive and one negative sample. Return the list of [FPR, TPR] points. Signature: def roc_points(y_true, scores):
code.reference_solution:
def roc_points(y_true, scores):
    P = sum(1 for y in y_true if y == 1)
    N = sum(1 for y in y_true if y == 0)
    pairs = sorted(zip(scores, y_true), key=lambda x: -x[0])
    points = [[0.0, 0.0]]
    tp = fp = 0
    prev = None
    for s, y in pairs:
        if prev is not None and s != prev:
            points.append([round(fp / N, 6), round(tp / P, 6)])
        if y == 1:
            tp += 1
        else:
            fp += 1
        prev = s
    points.append([round(fp / N, 6), round(tp / P, 6)])
    return points
